name: Adult orthodontics for looks

card.summary: Straightening teeth and correcting bite in adulthood with braces or clear aligners to improve the smile and lower face.
card.note: Teeth can drift back without retainers; adults may have periodontal and bone factors to plan around.

quick.overview:
Adult orthodontics moves teeth into better alignment using braces, lingual braces or clear aligners after growth has finished. People pursue it to fix crowding, gaps, overbite or crossbite, which changes the smile and how the lower face and profile look.

Reviews describe adults as motivated, cooperative patients, with the caveat that adult expectations can be high and need to be discussed at the start. Treatment typically takes one to two years, and jaw surgery is an option for severe skeletal cases when growth is complete.
quick.how: Treatment begins with an orthodontist's assessment, then braces (metal, ceramic or on the tongue side) or removable clear aligners worn for the prescribed hours. Appointments are spread every four to ten weeks for braces, and retainers follow treatment. One forum user planning treatment asked about aligner brands and budgeted several thousand dollars.
quick.risks: Reported issues include decalcification and decay with poor hygiene, root resorption, gum and periodontal considerations in adults, and relapse; over half of patients show some tooth movement back within ten years, which is why retainers are used. Jaw surgery carries surgical risks.

lead: Adult orthodontics is orthodontic treatment carried out after growth has finished, using fixed braces, lingual braces or clear aligners to straighten teeth and correct bite problems.[1][2] Adults seek it for appearance, function or as preparation for restorative work.[3][4] For looks, the chain is direct: appliances move the teeth, alignment, overbite or crossbite improve, and the smile and the way the lower face and profile read become more balanced.

A looksmax.org user in his twenties described a minor overbite and crossbite visible in side profile and a mouth that moved to one side when speaking, and asked about aligner options on a budget of five to eight thousand dollars.[5] Questions of this kind, about cost, which appliance, and whether tooth movement changes symmetry, are the typical form the topic takes in looksmaxxing discussion.

The scale of adult treatment is considerable. The American Association of Orthodontists reported that adults aged 18 and over reached a record 1,225,850 patients among its members in 2012, with men making up 44 percent of adult patients, and in a satisfaction survey 75 percent of adults reported better career or personal relationships they linked to their improved smile.[27] Literature on adult patients describes them as highly motivated, with expectations that are discussed at the start of treatment.[1][6]

Research includes systematic reviews of how treatment affects smile attractiveness, narrative reviews of adult-specific issues such as periodontal health and age-related bone changes, randomised and registered trials of techniques to speed tooth movement, and a large body of work on clear aligners.[6][11][12][13][16][28]

chain: Smile and lower-face profile look more balanced
angle.text: Moving the teeth changes visible alignment and bite, which changes the smile and can change profile appearance. Severe skeletal discrepancies may involve jaw surgery rather than tooth movement alone.

paras: Adult cases differ from adolescent ones because bones adjust less readily and gum and periodontal health, missing teeth, existing crowns and temporomandibular issues need planning.[1][3][6] Appliances include metal and ceramic braces, lingual braces and clear aligners; a consensus statement from the Angle Society of Europe addresses aligner treatment.[7][8] Bonding brackets to porcelain restorations is a recognized technical issue in adults.[9]

Treatment targets the problems classified as malocclusion: crowding (graded mild, moderate or severe by the space needed), overbite and overjet, crossbite, open bite and Angle's Class I, II and III molar relationships. Roughly 30 percent of people have a malocclusion considered severe enough to benefit from treatment, and some malocclusions accompany skeletal jaw disharmony, which can change facial shape.[26] Poor dental aesthetics can affect self-esteem, which is one reason adults seek treatment.[26]

Attempts to align crowded teeth date to antiquity, and the modern specialty traces to Edward Angle, who began influencing the field around 1890, devised the first basic classification of malocclusion and is called the father of modern orthodontics; his edgewise appliance appeared in 1928.[10] The American Dental Association recognised orthodontics as a specialty in the 1950s.[10] Until the mid-1970s braces were made by wrapping metal bands around each tooth; adhesives then made bonded brackets possible, and in 1976 Lawrence Andrews introduced the pre-adjusted straight-wire appliance.[10]

Lingual braces, fixed to the tongue side of the teeth for near invisibility, were developed by Craven Kurz and Jim Mulick in the United States in 1975-76, lost popularity by 1989 because of clinical difficulties, and saw a resurgence from about 2008 with digital and laboratory advances.[24]

Clear aligners changed the adult market. Align Technology was founded in 1997 by Stanford classmates Zia Chishti and Kelsey Wirth; Chishti conceived the idea of a series of devices moving teeth in small steps while he was himself an adult orthodontic patient.[20][22] The FDA approved Invisalign in 1998, sales began in 1999, and the company listed on Nasdaq in January 2001; a 2000 television campaign was described by the New York Times as the most aggressive consumer advertising plan the dental profession had seen.[22][29] Patents began to expire in October 2017, opening the market to competitors, and Align reported more than 18 million patients treated by 2017.[22][29]

Direct-to-consumer aligners followed. SmileDirectClub launched in 2014 with a remote model in which licensed dentists reviewed impression kits, listed on Nasdaq in September 2019, and filed for bankruptcy in September 2023 before ceasing operations in December 2023.[20][21] The American Association of Orthodontists filed complaints with 36 state dental boards and issued a consumer alert about such services.[20][21]

Wikipedia notes braces usually last one to three years and retainers are worn long term because over 50 percent of patients show some relapse within ten years.[10] Appointments are typically every four to ten weeks, and after braces patients usually wear a retainer full-time for about six months and then at night for many years.[10] If skeletal growth is complete, jaw surgery is an option for severe cases.[10]

Clear aligners are removable thermoplastic trays, designed through software that models each stage of tooth movement; each tray moves teeth a fraction of a millimetre, is worn about 22 hours a day, and treatment averages around 13.5 months.[20] Small tooth-coloured attachments may be bonded to teeth to help movement.[20] Reviews describe aligners as working reasonably for mild to moderate crowding or spacing of the front teeth and as less effective than conventional braces for some movements such as large rotations or correcting front-to-back discrepancies, and a 2014 systematic review concluded the available studies were not of sufficient quality for firm conclusions about effectiveness.[20] A 2024 narrative review addresses aligner stability and success.[11]

Lingual braces are nearly invisible; a 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis reported more tongue pain, harder hygiene and speech and eating difficulty than with conventional appliances, and speech typically improves within two to three weeks of placement.[24] Other review articles discuss accelerated tooth movement using surgical techniques and age-related alveolar bone changes in adults.[12][13]

Where the jaws themselves are mismatched, orthodontics is combined with orthognathic surgery, in which the jaw bones are cut and repositioned; presurgical orthodontics traditionally takes up to a year, newer approaches include surgery-first and aligners, and careful coordination between surgeon and orthodontist is described as essential.[23] Reported complications of orthognathic surgery include bleeding, swelling, infection and nerve injury, with numbness usually temporary.[23]

Systematic reviews have looked at how treatment changes perceived attractiveness. A 2011 systematic review of 20 studies in The Angle Orthodontist found that a dental midline deviation of about 2.2 mm was acceptable to both orthodontists and laypeople, that extraction and nonextraction protocols had no predictable effect on overall smile aesthetics, and that studies using real subjects found buccal corridor size and smile arc alone did not significantly affect smile attractiveness.[28]

The profile effect depends on the case. Tooth movement alone changes the position of the lips and teeth, while skeletal discrepancies involve the jaws and, when growth is complete, may be addressed with surgery combined with orthodontics.[10][23][26]

Surveys and reviews examine what adult patients want, how they comply, and the relationship between treatment and satisfaction.[14][15] A review of 1995 noted adult demand was rising.[1] In the 2013 AAO release, 71 percent of surveyed adults had worried before treatment about how others would see them, how they would look or whether they were too old, and most said the concerns faded once treatment started; 92 percent said they would recommend treatment to other adults.[27]

Reported issues include decalcification and decay with poor hygiene, which is why fixed appliances are less preferred where hygiene is poor, along with root resorption, periodontal considerations in adults and relapse.[10][3][6] Reviews note that adult patients need gum and periodontal health assessed before tooth movement.[3] Direct-to-consumer services without an in-person dentist drew criticism from the orthodontic community, and the collapse of SmileDirectClub left many customers without support.[20][21]

On looksmax.org, an adult user asked about low-cost aligners for overbite and crossbite and whether removing wisdom teeth would improve symmetry; one reply reported noticing no change five months after their own removal.[5]

The idea that wisdom teeth push the front teeth into crowding has a long history in dentistry. Encyclopedic summaries now say, based on recent research, that wisdom teeth alone do not cause crowding, and that removal for orthodontic reasons is disputed.[25] Prophylactic removal of disease-free wisdom teeth is itself debated, and nerve damage, temporary in about 1 in 85 patients and permanent in about 1 in 300 extractions according to one summary, is a recognised risk.[25]

Adult orthodontics also appears in forum discussions alongside jaw surgery and other facial-structure topics, where members ask whether tooth movement can substitute for skeletal change; these are individual questions rather than published findings.[5]

Controlled studies in adults include a randomized trial of alternating maxillary expansion and constriction in young adults and registered trials of piezoelectric corticotomy to speed tooth movement.[16][17][18] A registered study assesses psychological factors in adults seeking treatment.[19] Systematic reviews address smile attractiveness after treatment and the stability of clear aligners.[11][28]

lore.intro: Forum discussion focuses on cost, aligner brands and effects on symmetry and profile.[5]

claims.claim: Removing wisdom teeth can improve facial symmetry
claims.believers: A user planning removal asked whether it would help symmetry.[5]
claims.experts: No study in the cited material tests this; one replying user reported no change, and encyclopedic summaries say wisdom teeth alone do not cause crowding.[5][25]

claims.claim: Straightening teeth in adulthood improves how attractive the smile and face look
claims.believers: Adult patients report better relationships and confidence after treatment; in an AAO survey 75 percent linked improved career or personal relationships to their smile.[27]
claims.experts: A 2011 systematic review of 20 studies examined smile attractiveness factors such as midline position and found midline deviation of about 2.2 mm acceptable to laypeople and orthodontists; the AAO figures come from a member survey.[27][28]

claims.claim: Adults are too old for braces
claims.believers: AAO's president said many adults hid their teeth for years because they believed they were too old; adult patient numbers rose 14 percent from 2010 to 2012.[27]
claims.experts: Reviews describe adult treatment as feasible with planning for periodontal health, bone changes and expectations.[1][6][13]

claims.claim: Clear aligners do everything braces do
claims.believers: Aligner marketing and users highlight near-invisibility and convenience.[20][29]
claims.experts: Reviews describe good results for mild to moderate front-teeth crowding or spacing and less effectiveness than braces for some movements; a 2014 systematic review found studies insufficient for firm conclusions.[11][20]

claims.claim: Mail-order aligners are a cheaper equivalent to in-office treatment
claims.believers: Direct-to-consumer companies offered remote dentist review and lower prices.[21]
claims.experts: The AAO filed complaints with 36 state dental boards and issued a consumer alert, and the leading company shut down in 2023.[20][21]

claims.claim: Teeth stay where they are put once braces come off
claims.believers: Some users assume treatment results are permanent once appliances come off; orthodontic literature addresses retention for this reason.[10]
claims.experts: Over 50 percent of patients show some relapse within ten years, which is why retainers are prescribed long term.[10]

claims.claim: Jaw problems can be solved by braces alone
claims.believers: Some forum posters ask whether tooth movement can substitute for skeletal change.[5]
claims.experts: For severe skeletal discrepancies after growth, surgery combined with orthodontics is described as an option, coordinated by surgeon and orthodontist.[10][23]
